title: How Chromosome Pairs Make Different Mixes

scenes.tts: The first film showed why sex cells carry half the chromosomes. But if every sex cell gets half, why are those halves different? Return to the blue and gold chromosome pairs. This time, follow which member enters each sex cell.
scenes.caption: The first film showed why sex cells carry half the chromosomes. But if every sex cell gets half, why are those halves different? Return to the blue and gold chromosome pairs. This time, follow which member enters each sex cell.
scenes.visual: Hook first, no title. Rebuild the first film's large schematic parent cell with blue-and-gold long, medium, and short pairs. Several empty green sex cells orbit slowly outside it. A bright tracking ring moves from pair to pair as the question appears.
scenes.narration: The first film showed why sex cells carry half the chromosomes. But if every sex cell gets half, why are those halves different? Return to the blue and gold chromosome pairs. This time, follow which member enters each sex cell.

scenes.visual: Keep the chromosome pairs gently rocking. Overlay 'How Chromosome Pairs Make Different Mixes' for two seconds, then transform the title into a tracking label over one pair.

scenes.tts: A gene can have different versions. Each version is an allele. Put capital B on the blue chromosome and lowercase b on the gold one. A sex cell receives only one member of this pair. Each sex cell has an equal chance of getting capital B or lowercase b. Across many sex cells, about half carry each.
scenes.caption: A gene can have different versions. Each version is an allele. Put B on the blue chromosome and b on the gold one. A sex cell receives only one member of this pair. Each sex cell has an equal chance of getting B or b. Across many sex cells, about half carry each.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one pair. A B badge locks onto the blue bar and a b badge onto the gold bar at matching gene positions. The bars separate toward two green cells. Show '50%' beside each route on screen only, then repeat the separation with routes swapping sides.
scenes.narration: A gene can have different versions. Each version is an allele. Put B on the blue chromosome and b on the gold one. A sex cell receives only one member of this pair. Each sex cell has an equal chance of getting B or b. Across many sex cells, about half carry each.

scenes.tts: Now restore three pairs. During meiosis, each pair sorts by chance, independently of the other pairs in this model. The blue member may move left in one pair. In another pair, the gold member may move left. Each choice changes the final mix.
scenes.caption: Now restore three pairs. During meiosis, each pair sorts by chance, independently of the other pairs in this model. The blue member may move left in one pair. In another pair, the gold member may move left. Each choice changes the final mix.
scenes.visual: Rebuild three pairs vertically inside the same large cell. Rotate each pair independently around its center. Draw faint left and right destination lanes. Move one blue, then one gold, then another blue bar left, while their partners move right. Keep the model labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Now restore three pairs. During meiosis, each pair sorts by chance, independently of the other pairs in this model. The blue member may move left in one pair. In another pair, the gold member may move left. Each choice changes the final mix.

scenes.tts: One green sex cell now holds a blue, gold, blue pattern. Reset the parent cell and turn each pair again. Must the next sex cell match that pattern? Predict what the independent choices will do.
scenes.caption: One green sex cell now holds a blue, gold, blue pattern. Reset the parent cell and turn each pair again. Must the next sex cell match that pattern? Predict what the independent choices will do.
scenes.visual: Place the completed green cell at left with its three-bar pattern enlarged. Reset three neutral pairs in the parent cell at right. Let each pair slowly rock between orientations while a question mark grows between the old and new cells.
scenes.narration: One green sex cell now holds a blue, gold, blue pattern. Reset the parent cell and turn each pair again. Must the next sex cell match that pattern? Predict what the independent choices will do.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep both the old pattern and the unresolved rocking pairs visible. Do not reveal the next mix.

scenes.tts: The next cell need not match. A gold, blue, gold pattern is also possible. Each pair still contributes one chromosome, so every sex cell has half. What changes is which member arrives. Different eggs and sperm can therefore carry different mixes of alleles.
scenes.caption: The next cell need not match. A gold, blue, gold pattern is also possible. Each pair still contributes one chromosome, so every sex cell has half. What changes is which member arrives. Different eggs and sperm can therefore carry different mixes of alleles.
scenes.visual: Complete the new orientation and slide a gold, blue, gold set into a second green cell. Align both green cells side by side at equal size. A bracket confirms 'same chromosome number' while coloured pattern strips below them show 'different mix'.
scenes.narration: The next cell need not match. A gold, blue, gold pattern is also possible. Each pair still contributes one chromosome, so every sex cell has half. What changes is which member arrives. Different eggs and sperm can therefore carry different mixes of alleles.

scenes.tts: Chance does not promise exact halves in a small group. A short run can contain more copies of one allele. Across many model sex cells, the results should approach equal shares. An allele is not stronger because it appears a little more often once.
scenes.caption: Chance does not promise exact halves in a small group. A short run can contain more copies of one allele. Across many model sex cells, the results should approach equal shares. An allele is not stronger because it appears a little more often once.
scenes.visual: Use the same green cells as tally tokens. Build a short, uneven B-versus-b tally, then extend it with many smaller tokens until the two bars approach equal height. Label the display 'computed chance model' and keep both bars moving as trials accumulate.
scenes.narration: Chance does not promise exact halves in a small group. A short run can contain more copies of one allele. Across many model sex cells, the results should approach equal shares. An allele is not stronger because it appears a little more often once.

scenes.tts: Blue and gold mark two pair members, not stronger and weaker chromosomes. This model follows whole chromosomes only. In high school, you will add crossing over. Paired chromosomes can exchange matching pieces, creating still more allele combinations. That later detail does not change today's sorting rule.
scenes.caption: Blue and gold mark two pair members, not stronger and weaker chromosomes. This model follows whole chromosomes only. In high school, you will add crossing over. Paired chromosomes can exchange matching pieces, creating still more allele combinations. That later detail does not change today's sorting rule.
scenes.visual: Keep the blue and gold bars at equal size and brightness under a label 'colour tracks pair member'. Remove any winner symbols. Then place the whole-bar model inside a frame labelled 'today'. Outside the frame, show two bars swapping matching rectangular segments under 'later: crossing over', all marked schematic.
scenes.narration: Blue and gold mark two pair members, not stronger and weaker chromosomes. This model follows whole chromosomes only. In high school, you will add crossing over. Paired chromosomes can exchange matching pieces, creating still more allele combinations. That later detail does not change today's sorting rule.

scenes.tts: Mitosis does a different job. It keeps the chromosome number and makes matching body cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes sex cells with half and can make different mixes. Most asexual reproduction uses the copy path; sexual reproduction uses the sorting path.
scenes.caption: Mitosis does a different job. It keeps the chromosome number and makes matching body cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes sex cells with half and can make different mixes. Most asexual reproduction uses the copy path; sexual reproduction uses the sorting path.
scenes.visual: Split the frame with one carried parent cell at center. On the left, a 'mitosis' arrow duplicates the paired bars into two white matching body cells. On the right, a 'meiosis' arrow separates independently oriented bars into green half-set cells with visibly different patterns.
scenes.narration: Mitosis does a different job. It keeps the chromosome number and makes matching body cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes sex cells with half and can make different mixes. Most asexual reproduction uses the copy path; sexual reproduction uses the sorting path.

scenes.tts: Now the sibling puzzle has an answer. Each child begins from a different egg and sperm, usually carrying different allele mixes. The alleles stay separate rather than blending like paint. Sexual reproduction: meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.
scenes.caption: Now the sibling puzzle has an answer. Each child begins from a different egg and sperm, usually carrying different allele mixes. scenes.visual: Transform two different green egg-and-sperm combinations into two white fertilized cells. Grow each into a simple sibling silhouette carrying a small chromosome-pattern badge. Keep the badges distinct, then bring the exact rule onto one line as every pair settles.
scenes.narration: Now the sibling puzzle has an answer. Each child begins from a different egg and sperm, usually carrying different allele mixes. The alleles stay separate rather than blending like paint. Sexual reproduction: meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.

scenes.visual: One-line end card only: 'Sexual reproduction: meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.' No subtitle, site line, title, or teaser.
